definition:
The doctrine of creation confesses that God made everything that exists other than himself, freely, by his word, and from nothing, and that what he made was good. Creation is not God and not a piece of God, as pantheism holds; it is not an eternal rival to God, as some ancient dualists held; and it is not an accident, as a purely naturalistic account would have it. It is a gift, the work of a God who needed nothing and chose to give existence to what was not. It also depends on God at every moment: the same God who called it into being holds it in being. The Christian church confesses that the Father made all things through the Son and by the Spirit. The study of providence traces how God sustains and governs what he made, and the study of humanity traces the creature made in his image; this study follows the act of creation itself, the goodness of the world, and the hope of its renewal.

The Hebrew verb bara', ‘to create’, is used in the Old Testament only with God as its subject, which marks it as a word for divine making. The verb by itself does not prove creation from nothing, since it is also used of God creating human beings (Genesis 1:27), whom Genesis 2:7 says he formed from the dust. The doctrine rests on the whole witness of Scripture rather than on one word. Nearby verbs are 'asah, ‘to make’ or ‘to do’, the most general word, and yatsar, ‘to form’ or ‘to shape’, the word for a potter's work. Genesis 1:2 describes the earth before God's ordering work as tohu wabohu, ‘formless and void’, a rhyming phrase for what is empty and uninhabitable. In the Greek New Testament ktizō means ‘to create’ and ktisis means ‘creation’, either the act or the created world, or a single creature; kosmos means the ordered world. The Latin phrase creatio ex nihilo, ‘creation out of nothing’, is the church's name for the confession that God made the world without using anything that existed before it.
ot:
The Bible's first sentence is a confession: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). Most translations read it as a heading or a first act; some, such as the Jewish Publication Society's translation, read it as a temporal clause, ‘When God began to create’, which puts the weight on the ordering work of the following verses. Either way, Genesis 1 is striking against its ancient setting. In the Babylonian epic Enuma Elish, the world is built from the body of the defeated sea goddess Tiamat after a war among the gods. Genesis 1 has one God, no battle, and no rival. He speaks and things come to be. The sun and moon, worshiped as gods by Israel's neighbors, are unnamed ‘lights’ set in the sky to mark seasons (Genesis 1:16), and the great sea creatures that other peoples feared as monsters of chaos are simply things God made and called good (Genesis 1:21). Seven times God sees that what he made is good, ending with “it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). The pattern of six days of work and a seventh of rest (Genesis 2:1-3) gives the account its frame; how to read those days is the question on which Christians differ most (see below). Genesis 2 then retells the making of humanity at close range: “the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils” (Genesis 2:7), and he placed the man in a garden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15).

The goodness of creation survives the fall, though it is marred. After Adam's disobedience God says, “cursed is the ground because of you” (Genesis 3:17), and work becomes toil. After the flood God makes a covenant not only with Noah but “with every living creature” (Genesis 9:10) and promises that the rhythms of seedtime and harvest will not cease (Genesis 8:22). Israel's law roots its weekly Sabbath in creation, “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested” (Exodus 20:11), while Deuteronomy grounds the same command in the exodus (Deuteronomy 5:15). The pairing matters: the God who made the world is the God who redeems his people, and rest is a gift from both.

Israel's poets and sages praise creation more than they explain it. “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth,” and “He spoke, and it came to be” (Psalm 33:6, 9). Psalm 104 sings of a world teeming with creatures, all made in wisdom, and says that when God sends his Spirit “they are created” (Psalm 104:24, 30). Some psalms borrow the imagery of their neighbors' myths to deny their point, praising God who “crushed the heads of Leviathan” and “established the moon and the sun” (Psalm 74:14-16): what other nations told as a war among gods, Israel sang as the unchallenged work of the one Creator. In Job, God answers the sufferer with a tour of creation, “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4), a world whose wildness and beauty exceed human understanding and human use. Proverbs says “The LORD founded the earth by wisdom” (Proverbs 3:19) and pictures Wisdom as present before the world began, “a skilled craftsman at His side” (Proverbs 8:22-31), a passage the church later read in debates about Christ.

The prophets make creation the ground of both judgment and hope. Amos breaks into his warnings with hymns to the one who “forms the mountains” and “made the Pleiades and Orion” (Amos 4:13; 5:8). Jeremiah sets the LORD who “made the earth by His power” against idols that cannot speak (Jeremiah 10:12). In Isaiah 40 to 48, addressed to exiles in Babylon, creation is the answer to despair: the everlasting God is “the Creator of the ends of the earth” and does not grow weary (Isaiah 40:28), he calls the stars by name (Isaiah 40:26), he “alone stretched out the heavens” (Isaiah 44:24), and he “did not create it to be empty, but formed it to be inhabited” (Isaiah 45:18). The same God is “He who created you, O Jacob” (Isaiah 43:1), so that Israel's redemption is described as a new act of creation. Isaiah even says God forms light and creates darkness and brings both prosperity and calamity (Isaiah 45:7), leaving no second power beside him. The Old Testament's final horizon is creation renewed: “I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17), a world where the wolf lives with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6).
nt:
Jesus assumes the creation account and appeals to it. On marriage he reaches back past Moses' concessions to “the beginning of creation” (Mark 10:6), and he speaks of history as running “from the beginning of God's creation until now” (Mark 13:19). He points his hearers to the birds and the lilies as a lesson in the Father's care (Matthew 6:26-30). His own acts show him as Lord of what was made: when he calms the storm, the disciples ask, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” (Mark 4:41), and he multiplies bread and turns water into wine, doing quickly what the Creator does slowly in fields and vineyards.

The apostles then say what Genesis could not yet say: God made the world through his Son. John's Gospel opens by echoing Genesis 1:1 and says of the Word, “Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made” (John 1:3). Paul confesses one God, the Father, “from whom all things came,” and one Lord, Jesus Christ, “through whom all things came” (1 Corinthians 8:6). Colossians calls the Son “the firstborn over all creation” and explains the title at once: “For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” and “All things were created through Him and for Him” (Colossians 1:15-16). ‘Firstborn’, prōtotokos, here marks rank and inheritance, not that the Son was the first thing made, since the next verse makes him the maker of all created things. Hebrews says God “made the universe” through the Son (Hebrews 1:2) and applies to him the psalm that says “In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth” (Hebrews 1:10, quoting Psalm 102:25). Revelation calls Christ “the Originator of God's creation” (Revelation 3:14). The Spirit who hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:2) completes the pattern: creation is the work of the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Creation is also where the apostles begin when they speak to people with no Bible. At Lystra Paul and Barnabas urge the crowd to turn “to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them” (Acts 14:15), and at Athens Paul says, “The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth and does not live in temples made by human hands,” nor is he served “as if He needed anything” (Acts 17:24-25). In Romans he argues that God's “eternal power and divine nature” are seen in what he has made, and that humanity's root error is that it “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:20, 25). Hebrews states the doctrine of creation from nothing as directly as any text: “By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God's command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible” (Hebrews 11:3), and Paul describes God as the one who “calls into being what does not yet exist” (Romans 4:17). Against teachers who forbade marriage and certain foods, Paul insists that “every creation of God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4). Revelation's heavenly worship praises God because “You created all things; by Your will they exist and came to be” (Revelation 4:11).

The New Testament's last word on creation is renewal. Paul writes that “the creation was subjected to futility,” not by its own will, “in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay,” and that it groans “in the pains of childbirth” until the children of God are revealed (Romans 8:19-22). Through Christ God will “reconcile to Himself all things” (Colossians 1:20). The same language describes salvation now: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17; compare Galatians 6:15). At the end John sees “a new heaven and a new earth” and hears the one on the throne say, “Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21:1, 5). Christians differ on whether this means the present world purified and renewed or replaced; 2 Peter 3:10 is part of that discussion, since its Greek manuscripts differ on whether the earth will be ‘burned up’ or, as many modern editions read, “laid bare”. But the Bible begins and ends with God making, and its hope is not escape from creation but creation healed.

keyTexts.why: God creates the heavens and the earth by his word, orders them in six days, calls them very good, and rests on the seventh. The foundation of the doctrine.
The LORD God forms the man from dust, breathes life into him, and places him in the garden to cultivate and keep it. Creation seen at close range, with humanity's calling in it.
The Sabbath command is grounded in God's six days of work and his rest. Creation shapes the rhythm of Israel's life.
God answers Job by asking where he was when the earth's foundations were laid. Creation exceeds human understanding and belongs to God.
The heavens were made by the word of the LORD; he spoke and it came to be. Creation by word alone.
All creatures are made in wisdom and depend on God for food and breath; when he sends his Spirit they are created. Creation and its ongoing dependence together.
Wisdom is present before the world and rejoices in God's work. A passage the church later read in the light of Christ and debated at Nicaea.
The everlasting Creator of the ends of the earth calls the stars by name and does not grow weary. Creation as the ground of hope for exiles.
God promises to create new heavens and a new earth. The Old Testament's horizon is creation renewed.
The Word who was with God and was God made all things. The opening of Genesis is reread in the light of Christ.
Paul tells the Athenians that the Creator needs nothing and gives life and breath to all. Creation as the starting point for speaking to those outside Israel.
God's power and nature are seen in what he made, and humanity's error is worshiping the creature rather than the Creator.
Creation, subjected to futility, groans and waits to be set free from decay. The doctrine of creation looks forward to renewal.
All things were created in, through, and for the Son, hold together in him, and are reconciled through his cross. Creation and redemption meet in Christ.
The universe was formed at God's command, so that what is seen was not made from what is visible. The New Testament's plainest statement of creation from nothing.

history:
The first Christian thinkers taught creation in a world shaped by Greek philosophy. Plato's Timaeus pictured a divine craftsman shaping a material that already existed, and Aristotle held that the world had always existed. Justin Martyr, in the mid second century, could still speak of God making the world from formless matter, and scholars debate how much he meant by it. Within a generation the church's teachers were explicit. Theophilus of Antioch, writing around 180, criticized Plato and taught that God made all things out of nothing, and Irenaeus of Lyons, at about the same time, argued against the Gnostics that the one true God made the world himself, freely and from nothing, not through a lesser power working with inferior matter. Tertullian, early in the third century, wrote a treatise Against Hermogenes, a teacher who held that matter was eternal. The creeds made the confession universal: the Apostles' Creed confesses God the Father as maker of heaven and earth, and the Creed of Nicaea (325), as revised at Constantinople (381), confesses one God, maker of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made. The Arian controversy of the fourth century turned partly on creation texts, since Arius and his followers read Proverbs 8:22 and Colossians 1:15 as saying the Son was the first creature; the Nicene answer was that the Son is not made but begotten, and is himself the one through whom everything was made.

The church's great readers of Genesis did not all read the days alike. Basil of Caesarea preached a series of sermons on the six days, the Hexaemeron (around 378), full of wonder at the natural world. Augustine returned to Genesis several times, most fully in The Literal Meaning of Genesis (written between about 401 and 415), and argued that God created all things together at once, that the six days describe an order in creation rather than a sequence of ordinary days, and that God made the world with time, not in time. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), confronting the dualism of the Cathars, confessed that God is the one creator of all things visible and invisible, who made both spiritual and bodily creatures from nothing at the beginning of time. Thomas Aquinas taught in the Summa Theologiae (begun around 1265) that creation is not a change in some prior stuff but the giving of existence itself, and that while reason can know the world depends on God, that the world had a beginning in time is known by faith, not by demonstration; his contemporary Bonaventure held that reason could show it.

The Reformers kept the confession and read Genesis closely. Luther, in his lectures on Genesis (1535 to 1545), took the days as ordinary days, and Calvin, in his Commentary on Genesis (1554), stressed that Moses wrote in a way fitted to ordinary people rather than to astronomers. The Westminster Confession (1646) says God created the world from nothing, within the space of six days, and all very good. James Ussher's Annals (1650) dated creation to 4004 BC, a date later printed in the margins of many English Bibles. As geology in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries argued for a very old earth, Christians proposed several readings: the gap view, associated with Thomas Chalmers early in the nineteenth century and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), and the day-age view, which read the days as long periods. After Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859), Charles Hodge's What Is Darwinism? (1874) argued that Darwinism, because it excluded design, amounted to atheism, while B. B. Warfield at Princeton was open to evolution as a means of God's providence. The First Vatican Council (1870) confessed creation as God's free act, and Pius XII's encyclical Humani Generis (1950) permitted Catholic inquiry into the evolution of the human body while holding that souls are directly created by God.

In the twentieth century the debate took its present shape. Meredith Kline set out the framework reading in an article of 1958, and John Whitcomb and Henry Morris's The Genesis Flood (1961) launched the modern young-earth creationist movement. Francis Collins founded BioLogos in 2007 to advocate evolutionary creation, and John Walton's The Lost World of Genesis One (2009) argued that Genesis 1 describes God assigning functions to a cosmic temple. Alongside these debates, twentieth-century theologians such as Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics III/1 (1945), insisted that creation is the external basis of the covenant, the stage God built for his love, and Christians of many traditions have recovered the Bible's call to care for the earth as God's good work. The site's full survey of views is at /theology/doctrine/creation, with a longer treatment of the age of the earth and human origins at /theology/doctrine/origins.

differ.body: The days of Genesis 1 are ordinary days, each marked by evening and morning and numbered, and the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 give a real and fairly short chronology, so the earth is thousands of years old. Exodus 20:11 grounds Israel's ordinary week in God's six days, and the New Testament treats Adam as a historical first man (Luke 3:38; Romans 5:12). Defenders such as Henry Morris and John Whitcomb (The Genesis Flood, 1961) and Ken Ham argue that a global flood explains much of the fossil and rock record, and that death before the fall would make the world God called very good a place of suffering. They hold that the plain sense of Scripture should govern how the scientific evidence is read, not the other way around.

differ.view: Old-earth creationism and the day-age view
differ.body: The earth is billions of years old, and the Hebrew yom can mean a long period as well as a day (as in the phrase ‘the day of the LORD’), so the days of Genesis 1 are long ages or stages of God's work. God acted directly and repeatedly across that time to bring new kinds of life into being, without common descent. Defenders such as Hugh Ross, and before him Charles Hodge, who accepted the day-age reading, argue that God's works and his word cannot contradict each other, that the evidence of astronomy and geology points consistently to great age, and that this reading keeps both the trustworthiness of Scripture and the direct hand of God in creation. Some, such as C. John Collins, prefer to read the days as analogical, God's workweek described on the pattern of a human one.

Genesis 1 arranges God's work topically rather than chronologically. Days one to three form the realms (light, sky and sea, land), and days four to six fill them (lights, birds and fish, animals and humanity), with the Sabbath as the crown. Defenders such as Meredith Kline, Henri Blocher, and Bruce Waltke argue that the structure is plainly there in the text, that the sun appearing on the fourth day and the absence of evening and morning on the seventh signal a literary pattern, and that Genesis 2:5, which explains the lack of plants by the lack of rain, assumes ordinary providence was at work during creation. The chapter therefore makes no claim about the age of the earth; it teaches who made the world and for what.

God created life through the long process of evolution, including common descent, which he sustains and directs as its Creator. Defenders such as Francis Collins, Denis Alexander, and in part John Walton argue that Genesis 1 and 2 were never written to answer questions of mechanism or age, that the two accounts differ in order in ways that show their purpose is theological, and that the genetic and fossil evidence points consistently to common ancestry. Many hold to a historical Adam and Eve within early humanity, chosen by God as representatives, and they argue that God's use of a patient process is no less his act than an instantaneous one, just as providence in the womb is God forming a child (Psalm 139:13).

errors:
The church has rejected several accounts of the world's origin because they deny what Scripture teaches about God and his world. Dualism, found in Gnostic systems and later among the Manichaeans and the medieval Cathars, set a good spiritual realm against an evil material one, sometimes made by a lesser god. The church answered that the one good God made matter and called it very good; bodies, food, sex, and the physical world are gifts, not prisons (1 Timothy 4:3-4). Pantheism, which identifies God with the world, and emanationism, which pictures the world flowing necessarily out of God's being as light from the sun, both erase the difference between Creator and creature. Scripture presents creation as God's free act; he did not need to create and is not completed by the world.

Other errors deny that the world had a beginning or a maker. The ancient teaching that matter is eternal makes something other than God equally ultimate, and modern naturalism holds that the physical world is all there is and needs no explanation beyond itself. Deism admits a Creator but denies that he remains involved, a view treated in the study of providence. There are practical distortions as well: treating creation as divine and worshiping it, which Paul names in Romans 1:25, and treating it as raw material with no value except its use, which forgets that God called it good before any human being existed and that the earth is the LORD's (Psalm 24:1).
life:
To confess God as Creator is to receive everything as a gift. Breath, food, work, beauty, and the bodies people live in are not owed to anyone, and gratitude is the fitting response to them. Because creation is good, Christians are free to enjoy it without guilt and bound to treat it with care; because it is not God, they are free to study it, farm it, and build with it without fear. The same doctrine gives weight to every human life and to the created world together, since both belong to God.

Creation also shapes hope and prayer. Isaiah told exiles who felt forgotten to look up at the stars and remember that their Maker calls each one by name and does not grow weary. The one who made the world from nothing can raise the dead and make all things new, and Paul ties the two together when he speaks of the God “who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist” (Romans 4:17). A person who believes that has reason to pray about the whole of life, and reason to expect that God's last word over his world will be the same as his first: good.
questions: Genesis 1 describes God creating by his word, without any battle or rival. What difference does it make that the world has one Maker, who needed nothing, rather than being the product of conflict or chance?
The New Testament says all things were made through Christ and for him. How does that change the way you think about the natural world, and about Jesus?
Paul says every creation of God is good and that creation itself groans, waiting for renewal. How do both of those truths shape the way Christians should treat their bodies and the earth?
